title: The Hajj of the heart
hookLine: those who can't go share in it by fasting Arafah and by longing

cards: They came asking for something to ride. An expedition was setting out, and these men wanted to go, but they had no mount and no money for one. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told them he had nothing to carry them on.
Surah At-Tawbah keeps what happened next. They turned away, their eyes overflowing with tears, grieving that they couldn't find the means. The Qur'an says there is no blame on them.
They stayed home. Their tears went on the record anyway. Today, the Hajj of the heart.

teach.h: IF THEY CAN FIND A WAY.
teach.b: This path began the pilgrimage with a condition: the Hajj is due on those who can find a way. Today is for everyone else.
First, the men in tears. The verse doesn't scold them for staying home. It names their grief and lifts the blame.
Wanting to go and being unable is different from not wanting to go. Second, the people left behind.

Anas reports, in Sahih al-Bukhari, that on the way home from that expedition the Prophet told his companions: there are people in Medina who were with you on every road you traveled and every valley you crossed.
They were held back by an excuse.

teach.h: HELD BACK, AND STILL WITH YOU.
teach.b: Held back, and still with you. Third, a rule of thumb from the same collection. When a servant of God falls ill or travels, the Prophet said, the good he used to do while healthy and at home is still written for him.
The record follows habit and intention, not just location. Fourth, what people at home actually do.
On the day of Arafah, while the pilgrims stand on the plain, Muslims who aren't there are encouraged to fast, and Sahih Muslim records the Prophet's praise for that fast.

And in the first days of Dhul Hijjah, a person who plans to offer a sacrifice is told, in another report in Muslim, to leave their hair and nails uncut until it's done, a small echo of the pilgrim's restraint, kept at home, far from Mecca.

teach.h: THEY WERE HELD BACK BY AN EXCUSE.
teach.b: So while the plain fills, someone in an ordinary kitchen keeps the fast: their share of the day.

how: Muslims who cannot make the pilgrimage may fast on the day of Arafah, say the takbir through the first days of Dhul Hijjah, offer a sacrifice at Eid al-Adha if able, and ask God for the chance to go.

games.q: what does “the hajj of the heart” mean?
o: a Hajj made in Mecca with no rites, only prayer
the feelings a pilgrim has on first seeing the Ka'ba
taking part from home through longing, fasting and intention

games.q: the hajj of the heart — tap the pairs.
p: held back, and still with you
the good he used to do is still written

s: the Qur'an blames the men who stayed home because they had no mount
Surah At-Tawbah says there is no blame on them.
the Prophet said people held back by an excuse were with the travelers
Anas reports it in Sahih al-Bukhari.
only the pilgrims at Arafah can mark the day of Arafah
those at home are encouraged to fast it.

games.q: you came to the Prophet asking for a mount so you could go. he tells you he has none to give you. what happens next, by the Qur'an's telling?
o: they turn away in tears, and there is no blame on them.
they set out on foot anyway.
games.why: Surah At-Tawbah keeps their tears, and lifts the blame from them.

practice: If you pray, ask God in your own words for the chance to go one day, or for someone you love to go, plainly, the way the men who came asking for a mount asked.
If you don't, think of a place you've always wanted to stand in and couldn't yet, and let yourself want it, unhurried.

wordCard.voice: The Hajj of the heart. Taking part from home, by longing, by fasting on the day of Arafah, and by the intention of those who are held back by an excuse. Today's word.

orig.note: an excuse; those held back by one were 'with you' on the road.

carryVoice: Your line: longing counts. Being held back is not the same as staying away. Back tomorrow, same hill.
